opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are really two goals that have always been intertwined in my work, and in a lot of NLP more broadly. One is the scientific goal: understanding how language works, how people learn it, how meaning gets attached to words and sentences, and how language connects to perception, action, and reasoning. The other is the engineering goal: building tools that let people interact with computers, and with each other, through language in ways that are actually useful.

On the engineering side, the way I think about it is that language is an incredibly powerful interface. It's the most flexible tool humans have for communicating goals, sharing knowledge, and coordinating. So if you can build systems that really understand language, not just produce plausible-sounding text but connect what they say to the world and to what the user wants, that opens up a huge range of applications. You can describe a task instead of programming it. A system can explain its behavior to you. You can correct it in natural language when it gets something wrong.

What I find interesting right now is that the two goals feed into each other. A lot of the most useful engineering ideas come from paying attention to how people actually use language. We don't learn from a billion labeled examples; we learn from instructions, explanations, and feedback. And when we try to build systems that learn the same way, we often learn something about the structure of language and cognition along the way.

The other piece, especially now that these large models work so well, is that the engineering goal has to include making systems we can understand and trust. It's not enough for a model to be capable. We want to know what it represents, why it does what it does, and how to fix it when it's wrong. So a lot of what I think of as practical engineering these days is really about interpretability, controllability, and building models whose internal knowledge we can inspect and edit, so that the technology serves the people using it.

r001.rationale: The response describes useful language interfaces and systems that serve users, but it does not identify freeing people to spend more time on meaningful activities as a goal.

r002.rationale: The response mentions large models and contrasts human learning with a billion labeled examples, but it does not say that the currently most effective route relies on large amounts of language data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it in two layers, and I try to keep them separate even though they constantly feed into each other.

The first layer is the straightforward engineering one. There are things people want to do with language that computers are still bad at: following complicated instructions, explaining what they've done, learning a new task from a handful of examples the way a new employee would. If you can build a system that does those things reliably, that's valuable on its own terms, and you don't need a theory of mind or a theory of meaning to justify the work. You just need the thing to work, and to work in a way that people can trust and predict.

The second layer is the one I actually find myself drawn to, which is that language is not just the interface to these systems, it's also a window into how they, and we, represent the world. When you build a model that can talk about what it's doing, you've given yourself a tool for inspecting it. When you train a model on human language, you're implicitly importing a lot of structure about how humans carve up the world, and it's worth asking how much of that structure the model actually acquires versus just imitates on the surface.

So the practical goal, for me, is not just "make the system output good text." It's "make a system whose behavior is organized around the same kinds of abstractions that humans use," because that's what makes it controllable. If I can say "be more careful about dates" or "don't assume the user is an expert" and the system changes in the way I'd expect, that's because somewhere inside it there's a representation of care, or of expertise, that lines up with mine. That alignment of abstractions is the thing I think we should be engineering toward, and it's also, not coincidentally, a scientific question about what these models have learned.

Where it gets interesting is that the two layers sometimes pull in different directions. The fastest way to get a benchmark number up is often not the way that gives you an interpretable, steerable system. And I think the field has been a little too willing to accept that tradeoff. My own bias is that if you build the thing you can understand, you usually end up with the thing that generalizes better anyway, because what you've captured is the structure of the problem rather than the structure of the dataset.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliable, controllable systems and human-like abstractions, but does not identify giving people more time for meaningful activities as a goal.

r002.rationale: It says training on human language imports structure, but does not judge that the most effective current route depends on large amounts of language data.

astra-6.text:
I think the practical goal is to build systems that help people do things they couldn’t otherwise do, or make difficult things easier. Language is a really natural interface for that: we use it to explain what we want, share knowledge, and coordinate with other people. We’d like to be able to do those same things with computers.

But that means going beyond a system that can produce a plausible response. It needs to figure out what you’re trying to accomplish, recognize when it’s missing information, and ask a useful question. So I think of the engineering challenge as building tools that can participate in that process—tools that people can guide, correct, and reliably use to extend their own abilities.

r002.rationale: The response discusses language as an interface and describes capabilities helpful systems need, but it does not say that the most effective current approach relies on large amounts of language data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal is to build systems that help people do things they couldn’t do before, or make things they already do easier. Language is a particularly exciting interface for that because it lets people express what they want without having to translate it into a formal specification or a program.

But that means the engineering problem goes beyond building a system that produces plausible text. It has to understand enough about your goal, and the context you’re working in, to take useful action. And when it doesn’t understand, it needs to be able to ask a question or give you a way to correct it. So I think a lot about language technologies as components of a collaboration with a person, where success is measured by what that person can accomplish with the system.
